what: Westinghouse engineer Jim Sutherland's home-built ECHO IV computer, running household functions in his house, was made public.

sources.title: ECHO IV
sources.quote: It was made public for the first time in 1966.

note: Considered earlier appliance automation (1900s electric appliances, Monsanto House of the Future 1957) but those were not machines responding to occupants under computer control. ECHO IV is the earliest house run by a computer found; the exact 1966 date (April per CHM) rests on a secondary source and the CHM page could not be fetched.

what: ECHO IV served the Sutherland household's daily routines in his home through 1976.

sources.title: ECHO IV
sources.quote: The computer was working in the Sutherland's house until 1976, and was donated to the Computer Museum in Boston in 1984.

note: Same event as the demonstration; it was a one-off home-built prototype in real daily use for about a decade. No earlier real-household use found.

what: Stanley Works engineers Raymond and Roby designed an optical-sensor device that opened a door automatically; installed at Wilcox's Pier Restaurant, West Haven, CT.

sources.title: Automatic door
sources.quote: In 1931, engineers Horace H. Raymond and Sheldon S. Roby of the tool and hardware manufacturer Stanley Works designed the first model of an optical

note: Heron of Alexandria's temple doors (1st c. AD) were opened by fire-driven water pressure, not by a sensor detecting a person, so rejected. No contemporary 1931 report could be retrieved; only encyclopedic sources agree.

what: The Stanley optical door was installed in a West Haven, Connecticut restaurant for waiters carrying food.

sources.title: Automatic door
sources.quote: installed in Wilcox's Pier Restaurant in West Haven, Connecticut for the benefit of waiters carrying plates of food and drink

note: Installed and sold for $100, so a real use outside the lab. The first-pass 1960 Horton date is the first commercial sliding door, later than this.

what: Microwave motion detectors made sensor doors common in the 1970s.

sources.title: Automatic door
sources.quote: microwave motion detectors became common in automatic doors in the 1970s

note: Wikipedia only says detectors became common in doors then; exact year of routine public use not established (Horton commercial sliding doors from 1960 were mat-actuated).

what: ENIAC produced the first computer weather forecasts (Charney, Fjortoft, von Neumann).

sources.title: Numerical weather prediction
sources.quote: The ENIAC was used to create the first weather forecasts via computer in 1950

note: Richardson's 1922 hand-computed forecast was not computer-run and failed, so rejected. Automatic weather stations (e.g. a Friez/Bendix unit reportedly finished spring 1941, delivered to the US Navy 1942, per a 1947 USNI article that could not be fetched) are an earlier sensor-only candidate that I could not verify with a quote.

what: Rossby's group at the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute produced the first routine operational computer forecast.

sources.title: Numerical weather prediction
sources.quote: In 1954, Carl-Gustav Rossby's group at the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute used the same model to produce the first operational forecast

note: Earlier than the first-pass JNWPU May 1955 (which Wikipedia gives as the US start). Possible earlier operational automatic weather stations (1941-42) unverified.

what: Sidney Pressey at Ohio State built a mechanical machine that presented multiple-choice questions and scored answers without a teacher.

sources.title: Intelligent tutoring system
sources.quote: date back as early as 1924, when Sidney Pressey of Ohio State University created a mechanical teaching machine to instruct students without a human teacher

sources.title: teaching machine
sources.quote: inception (P571): 1920s

note: Dates differ across sources (1924 vs mid-1920s, one says 1926). Earlier mechanical test-scorers not found. It is mechanical, not a computer, but fits the definition (presents questions, grades answers).

what: PLATO I began operating on the University of Illinois ILLIAC I computer as the first generalized computer-assisted instruction system.

sources.title: PLATO (computer system)
sources.quote: Starting in 1960, it ran on the University of Illinois's ILLIAC I computer.

note: Pressey's machine saw only limited classroom/commercial use (Welch contract failed ~1929, not verified by a fetched quote). PLATO I was largely an experiment, so practical use is uncertain.

what: MYCIN, a Stanford expert system for diagnosing infections, was developed from early in the 1970s.

sources.title: MYCIN
sources.quote: MYCIN was developed over five or six years in the early 1970s at Stanford University.

note: Earlier candidates: Ledley and Lusted 1959 (Science) was a theoretical argument not a working system (Wikipedia Ledley article); Warner's 1961 Bayesian heart disease program and de Dombal's Leeds abdominal pain system (1971-72) are probably earlier or comparable working systems but I could not fetch a source with a quote. Date is approximate.

what: Weizenbaum's ELIZA/DOCTOR script, a computer program imitating a Rogerian psychotherapist, was published in 1966.

sources.title: ELIZA
sources.quote: In Weizenbaum's 1966 article, he described ELIZA as a system that applied a pattern-matching mechanism along with interchanging scripts

note: Pattern matching only; it does not assess personality or deliver real therapy. Colby, Watt and Gilbert published 'A computer method of psychotherapy' in 1966 (PubMed 5936301, not fetched) which is of similar date. PARRY (1972) simulates a patient not a therapist.

what: Cesare Lombroso used a device measuring blood pressure changes on criminal suspects in police cases.

sources.title: Polygraph
sources.quote: Early devices for lie detection include an 1895 invention of Cesare Lombroso used to measure changes in blood pressure for police cases

note: Earlier than Larson's 1921 polygraph. Lombroso measured blood pressure/pulse only, not breathing or skin conductance, so fit is partial; Benussi 1904 (breathing) and Mackenzie 1906 also precede Larson. Dating of Lombroso is secondary-source only.

what: Larson's polygraph, recording blood pressure and breathing, was first applied in law enforcement by the Berkeley Police Department.

sources.title: Polygraph
sources.quote: first applied in law enforcement work by the Berkeley Police Department under its nationally renowned police chief August Vollmer

note: Lombroso's 1895 police use may be earlier but is a less certain, single-signal device; Larson's multi-signal instrument is the first to match the definition and be routinely applied.

what: Hans Berger recorded the first human EEG in Jena.

sources.title: Electroencephalography
sources.quote: German physiologist and psychiatrist Hans Berger (1873–1941) recorded the first human EEG in 1924.

note: Caton recorded animal brain electricity in 1875 but not humans, so rejected. Berger published in 1929.

what: Gibbs, Davis and Lennox described EEG spike-wave patterns of epilepsy, starting clinical electroencephalography; first EEG lab opened at Massachusetts General Hospital in 1936.

sources.title: Electroencephalography
sources.quote: Gibbs, Davis and Lennox described interictal spike waves and the three cycles/s pattern of clinical absence seizures, which began the field of clinical electroencephalography.

note: Fisher and Lowenbach demonstrated epileptiform spikes in 1934; that is a research finding, not clinical service, so 1935 chosen. Berger himself used EEG on patients from 1920s but no clinical service is documented.

what: ATR labs in Kyoto reconstructed 10x10-pixel images a person viewed from brain signals.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: allowed researchers to reconstruct images from brain signals at a resolution of 10×10 pixels

note: Only seen images are decoded, not specific thoughts or memories, so it is a partial fit; Nishimoto 2011 movie reconstruction is later. Yang Dan 1999 decoded images from cat thalamus (animal, rejected).

what: Chang and Makin at UCSF decoded spoken sentences from ECoG signals into text with 3% word error rate.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: Edward Chang and Joseph Makin from UCSF reported that ECoG signals could be used to decode speech from epilepsy patients

note: Decodes overt speech from a 50-sentence set, not private thoughts; Willett et al. 2021 (attempted handwriting to text) is later and could not be quoted. P300 speller (1988) selects letters by attention, not thoughts. Poor fit overall.

what: Jacques Vidal at UCLA showed a noninvasive EEG visual-evoked-potential BCI after his 1973 paper.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: Vidal's 1977 experiment was the first application of BCI after his 1973 BCI challenge.

note: Fetz 1969 monkeys controlling a meter with single neurons and Grey Walter's 1964 CNV experiments are earlier brain-to-machine links; Fetz was animal biofeedback and Walter unverified, so rejected.

what: Kennedy and Bakay implanted a locked-in patient, Johnny Ray, who learned to control a computer cursor.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: Ray's implant was installed in 1998 and he lived long enough to start working with the implant, eventually learning to control a computer cursor

note: Birbaumer's slow cortical potential spelling device for paralysed patients (1999) is nearly contemporary; earlier lab cursor control with EEG (Wolpaw 1991) was not a service for patients.

what: Djourno and Eyries in France invented the original cochlear implant, stimulating the auditory nerve electrically.

sources.title: Cochlear implant
sources.quote: André Djourno and Charles Eyriès invented the original cochlear implant in 1957.

note: Earlier than the first-pass House 1961. Cardiac pacemaker implants (1958) are body implants not neural/sensory, so rejected for this concept.

what: Hochmair's multichannel cochlear implant was first implanted in a person in Vienna, followed by Clark's in 1978; both were commercialized.

sources.title: Cochlear implant
sources.quote: with the Hochmairs' device first implanted in a person in December 1977 and Clark's in August 1978

note: House/3M single-channel devices were marketed from 1972 and FDA-approved for adults in 1984 (not verified with a fetched quote), which may be earlier practical use. Date here is a weak proxy.

concept_note: Kept 1966 ECHO IV as demonstration and added same-date practical use; mass adoption (X10 1975, smart speakers ~2014-2019) not given because no fetchable source with a usable quote.
Confirmed the 1931 Stanley optical door as earlier than the 1960 Horton door; mass adoption only loosely dated to the 1970s.
Never realised; no fully machine-run city exists, so no milestones.
Numerical forecasts: ENIAC 1950 demo; practical use moved earlier to Sweden 1954. Automatic weather stations (1941-42) possibly earlier but unverified. No mass adoption given.
Pressey 1924 kept; PLATO 1960 added as low-confidence practical use. No mass adoption: Pressey's and Skinner's machines failed commercially.
MYCIN still the only quotable demonstration; probably earlier 1959-1972 systems unverified. No practical use or mass adoption sourced.
ELIZA 1966 kept as low-confidence analogue; no real computer assessment-plus-therapy system in routine use found, so no other kinds.
Added Lombroso 1895 as earlier low-confidence demonstration; Larson 1921 moved to practical use. Mass adoption (about 2 million US tests a year in the 1980s) not sourced.
Berger 1924 confirmed; clinical use 1935 added. Mass adoption not sourced.
Only partial matches (2008 image reconstruction, seen not thought); no true thought or memory reading exists, so no practical use or mass adoption.
Only speech or handwriting decoders exist, not thought-to-text; one low-confidence demonstration, no practical use.
Vidal 1977 demonstration kept; practical use 1998 added. No mass adoption.
Cochlear implant demo moved earlier to 1957 (Djourno and Eyries); practical use uncertain. Mass adoption not sourced.
Hypothetical only (Wikipedia: hypothetical process); no milestones.
